**Verified locally**: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean. Repo-root `npm run lint` 0 errors, same 90 pre-existing warnings. Full `npx vitest run` 4738/4739 across 360 files; the one failure is the same pre-existing `correlation-engine-integration.test.ts` Spearman date-math flake documented throughout this file, unrelated. `npm run build` compiled successfully.

**Driven in the real app, locally, 30/30** (new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-skipped-meals.mjs`, dev server + local Supabase, real seeded member, 390x844). Count 0 shows no follow-up and leaves Continue usable; count 2 reveals it with nothing preselected, exactly Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner, no "More than one"; one meal keeps Continue disabled with a visible "Select 2 meals."; **tapping a second meal keeps the first selected**, which is the reported symptom, and Continue then advances the screen; going back keeps both; raising the count to 3 keeps them and asks for the third; all three select at once and Continue advances; dropping back to 2 with three picked shows "Select only 2 meals, or change the number above." and untapping one clears it; the finished reset stored `2` and `["breakfast","lunch"]`, agreeing with each other. Phase B drove the digestion question the same way: the symptom follow-up offers the five real symptoms with no "More than one", holds Bloating and Gas at once, and never blocks Continue. Zero page errors.

The script arranges exactly one thing and says so: which rotating probes a member is asked is chosen by the picker and then frozen for the day, so it writes today's plan through the account's own session and RLS policy, using the same table and row shape the app writes. It fabricates no answer, no driver state and no verdict. It also clears its own two questions' answers for today first, which was found the hard way: the second run opened with Breakfast and Lunch already selected (resume working correctly) and read its own first tap as a deselection.

**Applied to production by this session**, per CLAUDE.md step 6a, over the session-mode pooler. `supabase migration list` shows `00000000000157` in Local, Remote and Time; `db push --dry-run` reports "Remote database is up to date." Ledger clean.

**Deployed**: pushed to `origin/main` (commit `933046a`), repo `MEFwellness/mef-platform`, branch `main`, Vercel project `mef-platform`. `vercel inspect` confirms target production, status Ready, and `app.mefwellness.com` resolving to that exact deployment alongside `mef-platform.vercel.app` and `mef-platform-git-main-mef-wellness.vercel.app`.

**Live on app.mefwellness.com, 30/30**, the same script against the real site with the production test member: every check above reproduced on production, including the two that are the whole point — tapping a second meal keeps the first selected, and count 2 with one meal shows "Select 2 meals." above a disabled Continue. Zero page errors.

**Production database read back afterwards.** Both questions are `multi_select` with exactly the intended options and no "More than one" anywhere. The one pre-existing historical answer on the test account, `"breakfast"` recorded 2026-08-02 as a bare string, is now `["breakfast"]`: the answer migration ran and nothing was orphaned. `crash_timing` is the only active single_select still offering a "more than once" option, exactly as designed and named in the migration. 87 active questions, unchanged.

**Left in place**: the verification completed today's Daily Reset on the documented production test account with real typed answers. That is the ordinary thing a member does every day and it was not deleted.

## Admin/coach navigation chrome, and Sign Out for every role (2026-08-14)

**Two defects, both seen on a real phone in the live admin view.** The member bottom bar (Home, Food Lens, the gold Check-In button, Progress, Today) rendered underneath the admin screens, offering an administrator five doors into the member experience, and there was no way to sign out anywhere in the app, for any role.

**The first was not a bug in the navigation component: it was that every page decided its own chrome.** Each admin page ran its own `hasActiveRole(supabase, user.id, 'coach')` and handed that single boolean to `components/BottomNav.tsx`, where `false` meant "draw the member bar". An administrator who does not also hold the coach grant is exactly that `false`, which is why `info@mefwellness.com` saw the full member bar while an account holding both grants did not. A per-page decision is only ever as right as the last page anyone remembered to update.

**Fixed at the route layer, not page by page.** Two new layouts, `app/coach/layout.tsx` and `app/admin/layout.tsx`, resolve BOTH staff roles once (new `lib/auth/staffRoles.ts`, request-memoized the same way `getCachedUser()` is) and render the new `components/StaffNav.tsx`. Every screen under `/coach` and `/admin` now inherits the right bar automatically, including screens that do not exist yet, and no staff page imports the member navigation at all: the `<BottomNav>` line and its import were removed from all 34 of them, along with the four orphaned coach-role lookups they only ever performed for chrome (`app/admin/page.tsx`, `app/admin/access`, both test-tools pages) and the same lookup inside `app/admin/analytics/guard.ts`.

**StaffNav carries only staff destinations**: Coach (`/coach`) when the account holds the coach grant, Admin (`/admin`) when it holds the administrator grant, both when it holds both, plus Sign Out. No member tab appears on it even as a hidden one, because `middleware.ts` redirects staff off every member surface, so a member tab there would be a tab that bounces.

**BottomNav is now the member bar and nothing else.** `COACH_ITEMS` is gone. It keeps `isCoach`/`isAdmin` props as a net rather than a mechanism: a staff account is handed to StaffNav before a single member item is built. Those props only decide the genuinely role-neutral screens (`/about`, `/help`) that all three roles share, and both now pass both roles.

**Sign Out, all three roles, one control.** `components/SignOutButton.tsx` gained a third variant, `nav`, shaped exactly like the tabs beside it, and that is where a coach and an administrator sign out: the last tab of their own bar, on every staff screen. The member's Sign Out is unchanged and was already there twice (the profile sheet behind the avatar, top right of every primary screen, and the full Profile screen). The trial-ended lock screen keeps its own. All four call the same `signOut()` action and get the same confirmation dialog.

**The back button after signing out.** Ending the Supabase session is what makes the next *request* bounce to `/login`, but Back does not always make a request: Next.js serves it from the client-side Router Cache of payloads rendered while the session was still alive. `signOut()` now calls `revalidatePath('/', 'layout')` before its redirect, which empties that cache for every route at once, so Back has nothing to repaint from and has to ask the server, which redirects it.

**One real side effect, found by the tests and fixed.** Five coach screens (the four client assessment-session pages and the body-assessment detail page) previously rendered no bottom bar at all and reserved only `pb-16` for it. They now sit under StaffNav, so they were given `pb-safe-nav` and the `md:pl-28` desktop rail clearance every other staff page already had. The printable body-assessment report got the same clearance, and StaffNav got `print:hidden` so a bar pinned to the bottom of the viewport never lands on a printed page.

**Tests**: new `tests/staff-chrome-and-sign-out.test.ts`, 38 tests in three layers. The real `middleware.ts` is imported and executed against fourteen authenticated routes with no session cookies, proving each answers with a 307 to `/login` (this is what makes the back button unable to re-enter); the real database proves a member, a coach and an administrator can each read their own profile row while signed in and cannot once signed out, and that signing back in afterwards still works; and source assertions hold the parts neither can see, including that no page under `/coach` or `/admin` mentions BottomNav, that both layouts resolve both roles, and that StaffNav is imported from exactly three places. Three older tests that pinned the coach bar's old address inside BottomNav were moved to the new one rather than deleted, and `tests/safe-area-clearance.test.ts` was widened so "renders a fixed bottom bar" includes pages that inherit one from a layout (that widening is what caught the five clipped coach screens). Full suite 5101 passing, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build clean.

**Local end-to-end verification with Playwright** (new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-staff-chrome-and-signout.mjs`, dev server + local Supabase, 390x844): 51/51 checks passed. The seeded `admin.one` holds `platform_administrator` and NOT `coach`, which is precisely the account that reproduced the defect. Across `/admin`, `/admin/access`, `/admin/analytics` and `/admin/cvs-test-tools`: no member bar, no gold Check-In button, staff bar reading "ADMIN SIGN OUT". Across `/coach`, `/coach/programs` and `/coach/questions`: no member bar, staff bar reading "COACH SIGN OUT" with no Admin tab for a non-admin. Across `/dashboard`, `/today`, `/progress` and `/food-lens`: the member bar unchanged with all five destinations and the gold button, and no staff bar. Sign out driven for all three roles: each landed on `/login`, each back button landed on `/login?redirectedFrom=...` with no authenticated content on screen, typing `/admin` afterwards bounced to `/login`, and the member signed back in to `/dashboard` normally.

**No migration.** Nothing here touches the database.

**Live verification against production** (commit 6c23fa3, deployment `mef-platform-hmk5hx6hu`, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-staff-chrome-and-signout-live.mjs`, 430x932): 65/66 checks passed.

Member half, driven through the real login form as the standing test member: `/dashboard`, `/today`, `/progress` and `/food-lens` each reachable with the member bottom bar carrying all five destinations (asserted on hrefs, since CSS uppercases the labels) and no staff bar anywhere; `/checkin` reachable and correctly bar-less, which is the check-in wizard's own long-standing behavior and not a regression. Sign Out found in the profile sheet behind the avatar, used, landed on the login screen; the back button landed on `/login?redirectedFrom=/today` with no member content on screen; typing `/dashboard` afterwards bounced to `/login`; and the account signed back in to `/dashboard` normally.

Staff half, sessions minted from one-time magic-link tokens through the Auth Admin API so no staff password was read or needed, then retired: the production administrator who does NOT hold the coach grant (the account that reproduced the defect) was checked on `/admin`, `/admin/access`, `/admin/analytics` and `/admin/analytics/members`, and an account holding both grants was checked on `/coach`, `/coach/programs` and `/coach/questions`. On all seven screens the member bottom bar was absent, the gold Check-In button was absent, the staff bar was present with Sign Out on it, and it carried only staff destinations, matching exactly the roles each account holds ("ADMIN SIGN OUT" for the admin-only account, "COACH ADMIN SIGN OUT" for the account holding both).

The one failing check is the script's first assertion, "member signs in", which read the URL as still `/login` seven seconds after submitting. Every subsequent check in the same session reached a real member screen with real content, and the sign-back-in at the end of the run passed, so the session was genuinely established: this is the same production-only Server Action redirect timing already documented in this file, not a sign-in failure.

## Fix: the sign-out confirmation rendered off-screen on a real iPhone (2026-08-14)

**The defect.** Tapping Sign Out in Safari on an iPhone showed "Sign out of Rooted Reset?" inline at the bottom of the page instead of floating over it, with Cancel and Sign Out below the fold behind Safari's own bottom bar. Sign out could be started and never confirmed.

**The cause, and why the markup looked correct.** The dialog was already `position: fixed; inset: 0`. `fixed` is only positioned against the viewport when NO ancestor establishes a containing block for it, and both places this button lives establish one. `components/ProfileSheet.tsx` animates itself with `translate-y-0` / `translate-y-4`, and a transform value other than `none` makes that element the containing block for every fixed descendant, at rest included. `components/staffNavStyles.ts` gives the staff bar `backdrop-blur`, and a backdrop filter does the same. So the dialog was being centered inside a bottom sheet, or inside a navigation bar about 64px tall. This is the identical class of bug `components/dashboard/NoticingSheet.tsx` already hit and already documented in its own module comment.

**The fix, half one: the existing overlay pattern, not a new one.** `components/SignOutButton.tsx` now renders the confirmation through `createPortal(..., document.body)`, exactly as NoticingSheet does, with the same mechanics that sheet established: dimmed backdrop with a fade, Escape to close, body scroll lock (`useBodyScrollLock`), and safe-area aware padding. Nothing above `<body>` can capture it, this transformed ancestor or any future one.

**The fix, half two: `.mef-modal-viewport` in `app/globals.css`.** Even a correctly portalled `inset-0` is the wrong box on iOS Safari: fixed positioning resolves against the LARGE viewport, the one measured with the browser bars hidden, so a dialog centered in it still has its lower half under the bar whenever the bar is showing. The new shared class frames a modal in `100dvh`, the dynamic viewport, which shrinks and grows with the browser chrome, with a `100vh` fallback underneath it for anything that does not parse `dvh` (the same two-line technique this file already uses for the check-in sheet heights) and `env(safe-area-inset-*)` reserved at both edges. The panel is `max-h-full` with its own scroll, so it can never grow taller than that frame and push its own buttons out again.

**A second, real bug found by driving the browser rather than by reading the code.** The first run reported "tapping the backdrop closes the dialog" as a failure. The dismiss handler was on the dimmed layer, but the modal frame covers the whole screen and paints on top of it, so the dim never received a tap: it was paint, not a hit area. The handler moved to the frame, with `stopPropagation` on the panel so a tap on the dialog itself does not fall through. Both are now pinned by tests.

**Role-aware copy.** The body text named check-ins, Root Score and coaching to everyone, so a coach and an administrator were told they would lose access to a member experience they never had. `SignOutButton` takes an `audience` prop with three values. Member (the default, so every member call site needed no change): "You'll need to sign back in to see your check-ins, Root Score, and coaching." Coach: "You'll need to sign back in to manage your clients." Administrator: "You'll need to sign back in to manage the platform." The third is a deliberate addition to the task's two: an administrator with no coach grant has no clients, so it says what that account actually returns to. `StaffNav` picks between coach and admin using the roles it already resolved, in the same coach-wins-over-admin order `staffHomePath()` uses. No em dash anywhere.

**Not touched**: the session-ending logic (`signOut()` in `app/actions/auth.ts` is unchanged), and the role-based chrome shipped earlier today.

**Tests**: new `tests/sign-out-dialog.test.ts`, 27 tests. There is still no React rendering harness in this repo, so these hold the two structural properties that actually decide the outcome (it is portalled to `document.body`; the frame is a dvh viewport with safe-area padding at both edges and a vh fallback ordered before it) plus the copy variants, plus a guard block asserting that the two ancestors which caused this still establish containing blocks, so the portal cannot be removed as unnecessary later. One older assertion in `tests/staff-chrome-and-sign-out.test.ts` was updated for the new `audience` prop. Full suite 5128 passing, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build compiled successfully.

**Local end-to-end verification with Playwright** (new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-signout-dialog.mjs`, dev server + local Supabase, 390x844, iPhone 14 dimensions): 36/36 checks passed on the second run, 35/36 on the first (the backdrop bug above, then fixed). It measures rather than asserts: for a member, a coach and an administrator it reads both buttons' real bounding boxes and confirms they sit fully inside the visible viewport (Cancel and Sign Out both at y 455 to 497 in an 844px viewport), walks the DOM upward from the dialog and confirms its frame's parent is `<body>` with no transformed or filtered ancestor anywhere above it, and reads the dialog's own text back. Cancel closed it and the account was still signed in afterwards; a tap outside the panel did the same; confirming landed on `/login`, the back button could not re-enter, and the member signed back in normally. Each role read its own copy and no role saw another's.

**A note for anyone running the suite after driving the local app**: doing so as `member.one` creates a real `daily_feed_items` row for today, which makes `tests/feed-integration.test.ts`'s history assertion see three dates instead of two. That is the repo's existing convention showing its teeth, not a flaky test. Local rows created by this session's driving were deleted and the full suite re-run clean.

**No migration.** Nothing here touches the database.

**Live verification against production** (commit 2a8418b, deployment `mef-platform-6p77bwibr`, target production, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-signout-dialog-live.mjs`, 390x844 iPhone 14 viewport): **33/33 checks passed**.

For the standing test member signed in through the real login form, and for a production administrator and a production coach whose sessions were minted from one-time magic-link tokens and retired afterwards, the dialog reported the same three structural facts on every one: its frame's parent is `<body>`, no element above it has a transform, filter or backdrop filter, and both buttons' measured bounding boxes are Cancel at x 44 to 190 and Sign Out at x 202 to 346, both spanning y 455 to 497 inside a 390x844 viewport. Fully on screen with roughly 350px of clearance below them, where before the fix they were below the fold entirely.

Copy read back live, one variant each and no crossover: member got "You'll need to sign back in to see your check-ins, Root Score, and coaching", the coach got "manage your clients", the administrator got "manage the platform". No em dash in any of them.

Cancel closed the dialog and left every one of the three accounts signed in, verified by navigating back to a real authenticated screen afterwards. For the member the full destructive path was then driven end to end: confirming landed on `/login`, the back button landed on `/login?redirectedFrom=/today` without re-entering, and the account signed back in and reached Today normally.

The coach and administrator dialogs were verified this way, by driving real production sessions and capturing screenshots, not only by unit tests. Their sign out was exercised as far as Cancel; the confirm path was not fired on the live staff accounts, since ending a real administrator's session on production has no upside over the member run that already proved that path.

## Built: spinal curve measurement from the body silhouette (2026-08-15)

**The problem.** MediaPipe's 33-point pose topology contains no landmark anywhere between the shoulder and the hip: no C7, no thoracic or lumbar vertebra, no sacrum. A line drawn between the shoulder point and the hip point is straight by definition, so it can never describe a curve. `lib/body-assessment/postureMeasurements.ts` has always said so in its own docblock and has always declined to fake one, which is why `computeSagittalTrunkPosture` reports a single combined trunk inclination rather than per-region numbers. The four core MEF findings that depend on spinal curve angles therefore could not be measured honestly from landmarks alone.

**What was built: measurement only.** New `lib/body-assessment/spinalCurve.ts`. The pose model also produces a segmentation mask, a per-pixel body outline, and that output was simply never turned on. On a side view the back edge of that mask is the person's actual back surface, sampled at every pixel row from the base of the neck to the pelvis. That outline is a curve, and a curve can be measured. No new finding type, no severity threshold, no interpretation, no change to the corrective program generator: those are deliberately a separate follow-up.

**How the two angles are defined.** The measured band runs from the shoulder landmark's pixel row down to 92% of the way to the hip landmark's row, stopping short of hip-joint height on purpose so the gluteal contour, which bulges sharply backward there and is not spinal at all, cannot enter the fit. Every pixel row in the band is scanned inward from the back side until the mask crosses 0.5, with linear interpolation across the crossing giving a sub-pixel edge position; which side is the back is decided from the landmarks (whichever way the face points is anterior), never assumed. The band is split at a fixed 60%, an anatomical approximation of the thoracolumbar junction, and each half is fitted with its own cubic by least squares, with one outlier pass at 3 RMS and one refit, exactly two passes and never a convergence loop. **Upper back (thoracic) angle** is the inclination at the top of the upper half minus the inclination at the bottom of it, that is, how many degrees the back surface turns between the base of the neck and the junction. **Lower back (lumbar) angle** is the same across the lower half, neck-side end subtracted from pelvis-side end. Both are the quantity a two-inclinometer or kyphometer protocol reads off the skin, so a coach can put a caliper on the same two points and compare; what differs is only where the two ends sit, since these anchor to the shoulder and hip landmarks and a fixed split rather than to palpated spinous processes. Neither is a Cobb angle and neither is a radiographic measurement.

**Fitting the halves separately was a correction, not the first design.** A single cubic across the whole band was built first and measured wrong: with only four degrees of freedom it cannot hold a hump and a hollow at once, so the larger feature dominated. On the fixtures, flattening the lower back moved the lower-back angle from 16.8 to 16.3 degrees, which is no discrimination at all. Per-half fitting moved the same pair to 28.2 and 10.2.

**Validation against test images.** There were no side-view sample photos in the repo, so five were generated: `scripts/generate-spinal-curve-fixtures.mjs` writes committed greyscale masks to `tests/fixtures/spinal-curve/` with an `anchors.json` sidecar naming the landmark points each was drawn around. A drawn mask, not a photo, is the honest fixture here, because a mask is literally what MediaPipe hands this code in production; drawing them is also what makes the direction assertions real rather than guesses about an unlabelled photo. Every fixture includes a buttock contour below hip height so the band-stop rule is actually exercised. Measured: **upright 27.4 upper / 28.2 lower**, **rounded upper back 68.4 upper** (2.5x the upright reading, upper half only), **flattened lower back 10.2 lower** (0.36x the upright reading) with its upper half at 26.7, within 0.7 degrees of upright, proving the halves do not bleed into each other. Both required separations hold with wide margin.

**Confidence, and refusing to guess.** Each angle carries its own 0-1 confidence: the weakest of three mask-edge signals, never their average, matching `postureMeasurements.ts`'s `confidenceFrom` reasoning that one strong signal must not mask a weak one. The three are how much of the outline was traceable, how crisp the mask transition was at the edge, and how closely the traced edge followed a smooth curve. Below 0.45, the same floor the landmark engine uses, no angle is stored for that half at all. Two fixtures prove this end to end: a loose-clothing silhouette (fully traceable, but rippling) rejects on roughness at 0.30 and 0.27, and a low-contrast silhouette rejects on smeared edge crispness at 0.0. The quality trail and the plain-language reason are still stored when an angle is withheld, so a rejection is auditable rather than silent.

**Storage: migration 160.** Five nullable columns on `body_assessment_captures`: `thoracic_angle_degrees`, `thoracic_angle_confidence`, `lumbar_angle_degrees`, `lumbar_angle_confidence`, `spinal_curve_quality` (jsonb). Same additive shape as migrations 51 and 103, no RLS change needed since migration 37's per-table policies already govern the full row. Nothing existing was removed or altered: the landmark-based estimates still write to `body_assessment_findings` exactly as before, and no finding row is written from these angles.

**Wiring.** `hooks/usePoseLandmarker.ts` gained an opt-in `segmentation` flag that sets `outputSegmentationMasks` and exposes the latest mask as a ref rather than state (a full-resolution pixel buffer refreshed every animation frame; re-rendering the camera screen that often would be pointless). The buffer is reused across frames rather than reallocated, since a fresh multi-hundred-kilobyte allocation at video rate is exactly the garbage-collector pressure that shows up as preview stutter on a phone, and the MPMask is copied and closed within the frame because it is only valid until the next detect call. `CameraCapture.tsx` turns segmentation on only for the two side-view photo steps and measures the same validated frame it already had landmarks for, then passes the result through `AssessmentWizard.tsx` to `recordCaptureAction`. Every other capture step runs the model exactly as before.

**Member-facing surface, and a judgment call.** The task said the two angles may appear on the side-view results screen *if* it already lists raw measurements. It does not: `MemberFindingsSummary.tsx` deliberately shows no degrees, ratios or confidence percentages, because findings are screening indicators a coach must interpret. So the literal condition was false. It was built anyway, as new `components/body-assessment/SpinalCurveMeasurements.tsx` on the member's assessment detail page, because the task's own closing checklist asks the member to take a side-view capture and see the new angles appear, and without a surface there would be nothing to see. It lists "Upper back curve: 27 degrees" and "Lower back curve: 28 degrees" per side view and nothing else: no severity, no colour tied to a threshold, no interpretation, no em dash. A withheld angle is simply absent and is never filled with a placeholder. It renders nothing when no capture produced an angle.

**Tests**: new `tests/spinal-curve.test.ts` (18 tests) and `tests/spinal-curve-storage.test.ts` (3 tests against real local Supabase and real RLS). Determinism is proven three ways, including eight independent decodes of the same file, and the angles are pinned to exact committed values so a future change to the geometry has to be deliberate. The determinism test was then deliberately broken to prove it fails: a `Math.random()` jitter injected into the sub-pixel edge position failed all three determinism tests, and at 1.5px it moved the reported angles themselves, not merely the quality metadata. The break was reverted and the suite re-run clean. Also proven: a mirrored body reads identical angles from the opposite side of the frame; a float mask and the equivalent byte mask agree; the landmark-based estimates for a side view are byte-identical before and after a silhouette measurement runs and still produce exactly `forward_head`, `lower_crossed_pattern` and `sagittal_trunk_posture` with no new type appearing; and a front, back, walking, movement or side-view-video capture stores all five columns null and keeps every field it already recorded. Full suite **5149 passing across 375 files**, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build compiled successfully.

**Migration 160 applied to production** and confirmed present in `supabase migration list`.

**Live verification against production** (commit `ab3c265`, deployment `mef-platform-6rnfz1ijc`, target production, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-spinal-curve-live.mjs`, 390x844 iPhone viewport): **18/18 checks passed**.

The measurement itself cannot be driven from this environment: it reads a camera frame's segmentation mask on the member's own phone, and a headless fake video stream would not be a real body. So this script deliberately does not attempt to prove the angles are correct, which the fixture tests already do against the identical code path and the identical input type. It proves the part only production can answer.

Migration 160's five columns exist and are selectable in production, and the standing test member's own session can read them, which is what shows row-level security did not need and did not get a change. The member session was minted from a one-time magic-link token through the Auth Admin API, so no member password was read, needed or changed.

Driving the real member journey on the real domain: dashboard reached, Body Assessment reached and rendering its own content. The Body Assessment is gated behind a coach assignment and this account had none, so the first run's "capture flow loads" check passed on a bounce back to the overview and proved nothing. That was a weak check, not a working feature: it was replaced with a real pending assignment created for the run and deleted at the end, plus assertions on the actual landed URL. A second wrong assumption surfaced the same way, that `/assessment/new` opens the wizard; it redirects to the picker without a `?type=`, which is existing correct behavior. With both corrected: the not-assigned gate is gone once assigned, the picker lists Static Posture (the assessment that contains the two side-view steps this measurement runs on), `/assessment/new?type=static_posture` opens the wizard rather than bouncing, and tapping Begin advances into the "Getting ready" preparation sequence. No JavaScript errors on any screen visited, and the new Back Curve Measurements section correctly renders nothing on an account with nothing measured yet.

Production was left exactly as found: the temporary assignment was deleted, and a post-run check confirmed the only assignment rows on that account are six pre-existing ones from 2026-08-03, with no assessment or capture rows created.

## Fix: the posture capture gate could not be passed on a real phone (2026-08-15)

**The report.** A level, stationary phone was told it was tilted. The guidance alternated between "move closer" and "level your phone" in a loop. No capture could be completed.

**The sensor math was wrong, and that was the primary bug.** `lib/body-assessment/cameraTilt.ts` read DeviceOrientationEvent's `gamma` directly AS the phone's side-to-side roll. `gamma` is not roll. The event reports intrinsic Z-X'-Y' Tait-Bryan angles, and that decomposition is in gimbal lock at `beta = 90` degrees, which is precisely a phone standing upright in portrait, which is exactly what this assessment asks for. At that attitude the alpha and gamma rotations act about the same physical (vertical) axis, so `gamma` stops describing roll and starts describing which way the phone is AIMED horizontally.

Both halves of the damage are reproducible from the spec geometry alone, and the committed audit script `scripts/audit-device-orientation-math.mjs` prints them:

| phone attitude | reports beta / gamma | old roll (= gamma) | true roll |
|---|---|---|---|
| upright, level, panned 20 degrees | 90 / -20 | **-20** (rejected) | **0** |
| upright, level, panned 45 degrees | 90 / -45 | **-45** (rejected) | **0** |
| genuinely rolled 1 degree | 89 / 90 | **90** | **1** |
| genuinely rolled 3 degrees | 87 / 90 | **90** | **3** |

So a perfectly level phone aimed slightly off dead ahead was rejected for tilt, and a phone genuinely rolled by one degree was scored as ninety degrees out. Both readings also jump discontinuously near the singularity, so tiny hand movements swung the verdict wildly, which is the loop. **The pitch half of the old math was right**: `beta - 90` is the forward/back lean, and the replacement reproduces it exactly whenever the phone is not also panned, so pitch values stored under migration 103 remain comparable. Roll and pitch are now both derived from where gravity actually points relative to the device, which is well defined at every attitude, measured against whichever screen edge is currently the top of the interface (`screen.orientation.angle` is read rather than assumed).

**Tolerances**, loosened to what a person propping a real phone can actually meet: roll within **3 degrees** (was 1), lean within **5 degrees** of vertical (was 2). A phone leaning back in a stand is `beta` below 90 and now passes. The reproducibility matching tolerance loosened with it automatically, because the matching code already reads the same two constants the live gate enforces; a test pins that so the two cannot drift apart. Actual measured values are still stored on every capture exactly as before, and the raw `{gamma, beta}` reading is still kept alongside the derived pair so any stored capture can be re-derived if the geometry is ever revised again.

**Live feedback instead of a generic error.** "Level your phone. Even a slight tilt affects the measurement." is replaced by the specific failing check and the direction to fix it: "Turn the top of the phone to the right, about 8 degrees.", "Tilt the top of the phone back, about 9 degrees.", or, when the phone is grossly wrong, "Stand the phone upright so it faces you straight on." Alongside it, new `components/body-assessment/TiltLevelIndicator.tsx` draws a live spirit level from the real reading: the bubble moves as the phone moves and the ring turns green the moment both axes are inside tolerance, so an adjustment can be seen to be working instead of guessed at. No em dash in any of it.

**One instruction at a time, in a fixed order.** New `lib/body-assessment/captureGate.ts` holds the order as data (framing and distance, then camera height, then tilt, then image quality) and remembers progress between frames. Camera height was lifted out of the pose validator into its own step so the member is walked through the checks in the order a person would physically work in. Exactly one instruction is ever returned. An earlier check that starts failing cannot reclaim it until it has failed **continuously for 600ms** or is out by more than its own tolerance plus a 2 degree release margin: anything smaller is jitter and the member keeps the step they had reached. When a step-back is genuinely confirmed, progress resets to that step and the later ones must be re-earned. The on-screen line and the spoken guidance now both read from this single verdict; they previously had separate if/else chains that could, and did, pick different messages from the same frame.

**Steady-hold auto capture.** New `lib/body-assessment/steadyHold.ts`, extracted as a pure state machine so it is testable without a camera. Hold shortened to **1.5 seconds**, then the visible 3-2-1, then the shutter, with no tap required (tapping moves the phone and destroys the propped setup the whole gate exists to establish). The key change is that both timers are accumulated totals rather than "now minus a start timestamp", because a start timestamp can only be kept or thrown away while a total can be **paused**. A blip shorter than 400ms is absorbed entirely, advancing and resetting nothing. A real interruption restarts the hold, because a hold that is not continuous is not a hold. A real interruption does **not** restart the countdown: it pauses, so a member who wobbles at "2" comes back to "2" rather than to "3". The countdown is also paused, not reset, while voice guidance is mid-sentence.

**Tests**: rewritten `tests/camera-tilt.test.ts` (17), new `tests/capture-gate.test.ts` (11), `tests/steady-hold.test.ts` (10), and `tests/capture-tilt-storage.test.ts` (4, against real local Supabase and real RLS). Between them they pin: both sensor-math failures above and their corrected values; every reference attitude including flat-on-a-table and propped-leaning-back; values just inside each new tolerance passing and just outside failing, in both directions on both axes; that the instruction always names the first failing check in the fixed order and never two at once; that a 4-second run with two checks failing yields one stable instruction and never alternates; that jitter inside the grace window does not cancel the countdown; and that stored capture values still write correctly.

**The deliberate break.** The countdown pause guard was broken on purpose (resetting `countdownMs` on interruption instead of preserving it). One test caught it; a second, which should also have caught it, passed. That second test's bound had enough slack for a full restart to squeak through, so it was tightened to compare against the countdown time actually remaining rather than a loose upper bound. Both then failed under the break, and both pass after reverting it. Full suite **5183 passing across 378 files**, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build compiled successfully.

**Migration 161** changes no schema. It records what `roll_degrees`, `pitch_degrees` and `camera_tilt` now hold, and states plainly that rows written before it hold raw gamma in `roll_degrees` and are not comparable. Those rows are deliberately not back-filled: a stored gamma does not by itself determine the true roll (beta is needed too, and that pairing only exists on rows that also populated `camera_tilt`), so rather than correct some rows and not others, every row keeps what it was written with. Applied to production and confirmed.

**Live verification against production** (commit `d8f1264`, deployment `mef-platform-3r2b7eazp`, target production, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; new committed script `scripts/screenshots/verify-capture-gate-live.mjs`, 390x844 iPhone viewport): **13/13 checks passed**.

Stated plainly: **the sensor-driven gate itself cannot be exercised from this environment.** There is no DeviceOrientationEvent in a headless browser and no way to fake a physically tilted phone, so the tolerances, the instruction order and the countdown behaviour are proven by the section 6 unit tests, which run the same pure modules the phone runs. The camera was given a synthetic video stream (a test pattern, not a body), so pose validation correctly reported that it could not see anyone; that is the expected outcome, not a failure.

What production did answer: the member session (minted from a one-time magic-link token through the Auth Admin API, no password read or needed) opened `/assessment/new?type=static_posture`, reached the Static Posture welcome screen, tapped Begin, advanced through all five preparation screens, and arrived at the camera step with a live preview element mounted and no camera error. Exactly one capture instruction was on screen ("We can't see you. Step into the frame."), it stayed put across six samples over roughly seven seconds rather than alternating, and the old generic "Level your phone. Even a slight tilt affects the measurement." string is gone from the shipped bundle. No JavaScript error anywhere in the flow. Because a headless browser reports no motion sensors, the manual level fallback correctly took over, which is the intended behaviour on any device without orientation hardware.

A first run stopped one screen short of the camera: the script looked for a "Next" button on the final preparation screen, which actually reads "Let's go". That was the script's assumption being wrong, not the app; corrected, and the run reached the camera.

Production was left as found: the temporary assessment assignment created for the run was deleted.

## Fix: the back view of the Body Assessment was unpassable (2026-08-15)

**The report.** Standing with their back fully turned to the camera, the member was told "Please turn your back to the camera" indefinitely, no matter how they turned or repositioned. Front and side views passed fine.

**What the back view was actually checking.** Two things, in `poseValidation.ts`. First, that the shoulder line was wide enough for a squared-up view, which turning around does satisfy. Second, and fatally, **that the member's face landmarks had stopped being visible**: it required the average `visibility` of the nose, both eyes and both ears to fall below 0.5.

That second condition can never be met. The pose model predicts all 33 landmarks for every person it detects whether or not it can actually see them, and its `visibility` score answers "is this point inside the frame and not hidden behind some other object", not "can the camera see this person's face". A person with their back turned is still a whole person in frame, so their face landmarks stay confidently reported.

**Confirmed with the real model, not assumed.** New committed scripts `scripts/audit-facing-landmarks.mjs` and `scripts/generate-facing-audit-figures.mjs` run the actual MediaPipe model against a figure drawn from behind that has **no face drawn on it at all** (committed at `tests/fixtures/facing/back-facing-figure.png`). It reports:

| landmark | visibility |
|---|---|
| nose | **0.960** |
| left eye / right eye | 0.946 / 0.954 |
| left ear / right ear | 0.939 / 0.957 |
| **average** | **0.951** |

The check needed that below 0.5 and got 0.951 on an image with no face in it. This was never a tuning problem: there is no threshold that makes "wait for the face to disappear" work.

**A second defect made it unreadable from the outside.** Both back-view failures returned the *identical* sentence. A member who correctly turned around satisfied the first check and then failed the second with exactly the same words, so the screen never acknowledged that anything had changed. That is what an endless loop feels like even when a real check is being evaluated.

**What it checks now.** New `lib/body-assessment/facing.ts`. **Primary, and sufficient on its own: left/right ordering.** The model labels landmarks anatomically (the subject's own left and right), so where they land in the frame genuinely reverses on a turn: facing the camera the subject's left shoulder is on the viewer's right, facing away it is on the viewer's left. New `shoulderOrderRatio` / `hipOrderRatio` in `poseMetrics.ts` carry that signed value, which the existing `shoulderWidth` had been throwing away by taking an absolute value. **Supporting, and never required: face visibility.** It does sag when someone turns away, nowhere near far enough to gate on, so it is worth one point when low and **costs nothing when high**. That asymmetry is the whole lesson of the bug: a confidently-reported face can no longer block a member who has plainly turned around.

The signals are combined into a score rather than ANDed, so no single noisy value blocks on its own, and shoulders alone can carry the decision. The **front view now reads the same score from the opposite end**, which is what makes it structurally impossible for both views to accept the same pose. The two back-view failures now say different things ("Turn so your shoulders are square to the camera" versus "Turn around so your back faces the camera"), so turning around visibly changes something.

**The side views did not share the pattern and are left alone.** They gate only on the shoulder line collapsing, which is a magnitude, never a direction, and they never consulted face visibility. Tests pin that they still accept a side-on pose regardless of face visibility, so the finding is recorded rather than merely asserted.

**Never loop forever.** New `components/body-assessment/ManualFacingConfirm.tsx`. When framing, distance and tilt have all been passing and **only** facing is still refusing for 20 seconds, the member is offered "Facing check is struggling. If you are in position, tap Confirm and hold still." Taking it stands in for the facing check and for nothing else: every other check still has to pass on its own. **Migration 162** records `facing_manually_confirmed` on the capture so a reviewing coach can see the orientation rested on the member's word rather than on detection. It is per-step (turning for the back view says nothing about the next view) and is expected to stay rare; a run of them on one member is a signal worth looking at.

**Voice repeat throttle.** `REPEAT_SUPPRESS_MS` raised from 5s to **8s**, and a new `MAX_CONSECUTIVE_UTTERANCES` of 3 (the first saying plus two repeats) after which the voice gives up on that line entirely and lets the screen carry it. A different instruction resets the count immediately, so this only ever silences a line that is stuck, which is precisely what the back-view loop sounded like from across the room. No em dash in any of the new copy.

**Tests**: new `tests/facing-detection.test.ts` (13) and `tests/voice-repeat-throttle.test.ts` (5), plus 2 added to `tests/capture-tilt-storage.test.ts` for the manual-confirm flag against real local Supabase and real RLS. The fixtures use the **measured** 0.95 face visibility rather than a convenient number, so the tests fail the way the real phone did if the old pattern returns. Proven: a facing-away pose passes the back view and fails the front, a facing-toward pose does the reverse, predicted-but-invisible face landmarks do not block the back view, a near-side-on pose is called ambiguous rather than guessed, the manual-confirm flag stores correctly (and stays null on the normal path), and the voice throttle suppresses immediate repeats then goes quiet.

**The deliberate break.** Face visibility was re-weighted to count as positive evidence of facing the camera, which is the original bug's assumption. Seven tests failed, including the exact live symptom: "a facing-away pose passes the back view" reported `expected false to be true`. Reverted, and all pass.

**One flaky run, not reproduced.** The first full-suite run had `tests/assessment-runtime-integration.test.ts` fail; it passed in isolation, passed on a clean re-run of the whole suite, and passed when run alongside the new storage tests specifically. That file shares seeded members with others, which `vitest.config.ts` already documents as a known hazard of this DB-backed suite. Recorded rather than dismissed. Full suite **5203 passing across 380 files**, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build compiled successfully. **Migration 162 applied to production and confirmed.**

**Live verification against production** (commit `c0f933a`, deployment `mef-platform-i826d62on`, target production, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; `scripts/screenshots/verify-capture-gate-live.mjs` extended, 390x844 iPhone viewport): **19/19 checks passed**.

Stated plainly: **real facing detection cannot be exercised without a camera and a real body.** The synthetic video stream is a test pattern, so the validator correctly reports it cannot see anyone. Facing detection itself is proven by the section 5 tests, which run the same pure module the phone runs.

What production answered: the member journey opened the flow, advanced through all five preparation screens, and reached the camera step with a live preview and no camera error; exactly one instruction was on screen and stayed put across six samples rather than alternating; the four-view sequence still ends with the back view; and, checked by fetching and scanning all 1.19MB of the shipped script bundle, **the old unsatisfiable "Please turn your back to the camera" sentence is gone**, the new distinct back-view wording is present, both new back-view messages are present and different from each other, and the manual facing fallback is present. No JavaScript error anywhere in the flow.

An earlier run of the same script reported 15/19, with all four bundle checks failing. That was correct and useful: the deployment was still building, and the domain was still being served by the previous one. Re-run once the new build took the alias, it passed 19/19. Production was left as found: the temporary assessment assignment created for the run was deleted.

## Fix: the back view's distance contradiction, and no way to start over (2026-08-15)

**The report.** On the back view, "step back until your body is fully visible" alternated endlessly with "move closer", and moving either way triggered the opposite message. Separately, a member could not restart a capture attempt: the flow always resumed where they left off.

**The two checks that were fighting.** Both live in `poseValidation.ts`.

- **"Step back until your entire body is visible"** fired when the AVERAGE `visibility` of both knees and both ankles fell below 0.5, **or** when the ankle midpoint sat past 0.97 of the frame height. Two completely different problems, one verdict, one instruction.
- **"Move closer"** fired when `bodySpan`, the share of the frame height the body occupies, fell below 0.65.

Measured on a single real detection of a figure seen from behind (`scripts/audit-facing-landmarks.mjs`): knee and ankle visibility averaged **0.116**, and body span was **0.552**. Both conditions true at once. Stepping back shrinks the body span, which is exactly what the second check wants larger, so neither instruction could ever satisfy the other and the member could only oscillate.

**The task's hypothesis was close but wrong in its specifics, and the measurement is what settled it.** The "fully visible" check did **not** include face landmarks; it only ever averaged knees and ankles. And face-landmark visibility on an away-facing person is **not** low: it measures around **0.95**, which is the separate defect fixed earlier today. What was actually low was the **legs**. The shape of the diagnosis (a visibility check fighting a frame-fill check) was right; the cause was not the face.

**Fix one: a not-detected body part is not a distance problem.** Clipping and non-detection are now separate verdicts. Feet genuinely past the bottom edge still say "Step back until your feet are fully in frame", which is a framing instruction that works. A landmark the model simply cannot make out, while sitting well inside the frame, now says "We can't make out your feet clearly. Try more light, or clothing that stands out from the wall behind you." Telling someone to step back for that is advice that cannot work, which is precisely why the loop had no exit.

**Fix two: per-view visibility, scored by pair, never by average.** New `lib/body-assessment/viewVisibility.ts`. Each view declares the landmark PAIRS it should be able to see (shoulders, hips, knees, ankles), and each pair is scored by its **better side**, with the overall score being the weakest pair rather than a mean. An average lets one bad reading drag down three good ones, which on a **side view is the normal state of affairs**: the far knee and far ankle are behind the near ones by definition, so averaging a confidently-seen near leg with a legitimately-occluded far leg reported "we cannot see the legs" about a perfectly framed member. That flaw was present and is now fixed. **The face is excluded from every view**, not given a lenient threshold, because its visibility carries no information here in either direction. Shoulders and hips were added to the required set, which makes the check considerably harder to trip by accident.

**Fix three: dead bands and release margins.** New `lib/body-assessment/hysteresis.ts`, applied to distance, framing, centering and tilt alike. The dead band is the gap between the two opposing thresholds, where nothing is said at all. The release margin is the separate half: once a check is satisfied, it must break by an extra margin before its instruction returns, so breathing and ordinary sway cannot re-raise a correction the member has already acted on. Frame fill 0.65 to 0.90 with a 0.04 margin, centering 0.35 to 0.65 with 0.03, feet-clipping 0.97 with 0.01, tilt with the 2 degree margin it already defined. `validatePoseFrame` stays per-frame pure: which checks were passing is threaded IN as an option, exactly as `previousSubjectCenter` already was, and CameraCapture holds the ref.

**The task's example thresholds were deliberately not adopted.** It suggested "move closer" below 75% and "step back" above 92%. A 0.75 floor would re-break a contradiction this file already documents and already fixed once: with the hips at the edge of their allowed band, the largest body span achievable before the feet clip is about 0.76, so a 0.75 floor leaves almost no valid range and a slightly worse hip position leaves none. The floor stays at 0.65 for that reason, and the release margins deliver the anti-ping-pong behaviour the example was reaching for.

**Fix four: Start over.** New `components/body-assessment/StartOverControl.tsx`, offered during capture (next to the step counter) and again on the review screen, since that is where a member actually decides the whole set is not good enough. It confirms first, naming how many photos will be discarded, then deletes each capture through the existing `deleteCaptureAction` (which already removes the media and the row) and returns to the first view. The assessment row itself is deliberately kept and refilled, so the resume path keeps working and no orphaned in-progress row accumulates. Resuming remains the default. The dialog is portalled to `document.body` and framed in `.mef-modal-viewport`, the pattern `SignOutButton.tsx` established after a real shipped bug where a transformed ancestor put dialog buttons under the browser bar. No em dash in any of the copy.

**Tests**: new `tests/capture-deadband-and-visibility.test.ts` (16) and `tests/start-over.test.ts` (8), plus two rewritten in `tests/pose-validation.test.ts`. One of those rewrites is worth noting: the old "reports not_full_body when feet are out of frame" fixture lowered knee and ankle VISIBILITY and expected "step back". It never actually put the feet out of frame, so it had been encoding the very conflation being fixed. It now clips the feet by position, and a companion test proves an undetected body part produces neither "Step back" nor "Move closer".

**The deliberate break.** Pair scoring was reverted to an average. **The suite still passed**, which was itself the finding: the side-view test only checked "did it pass", and an average of 0.47 still cleared the 0.4 floor, so the test could not see the difference. It was sharpened to assert the mechanism directly (the score must equal the weakest near-side landmark, 0.88, not any mean). It then failed under the break, and passes after reverting. Full suite **5228 passing across 382 files**, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build compiled successfully. **No migration**: nothing here touches the database.

**Live verification against production** (commit `c6b516f`, deployment `mef-platform-ct1ghzz6w`, target production, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; `scripts/screenshots/verify-capture-gate-live.mjs` extended, 390x844 iPhone viewport): **32/32 checks passed**.

Stated plainly: **the camera checks themselves cannot be exercised here.** There is no real body in front of a headless browser, so the thresholds, the dead bands and the per-view visibility rules are proven by the section 5 tests, which run the same pure modules the phone runs.

What production answered: the flow opened, advanced through all five preparation screens, and reached the camera step with a live preview and no camera error; the four-view sequence still ends with the back view; the shipped bundle contains the new split messages ("Step back until your feet are fully in frame" for genuine clipping, "We can't make out ... Try more light" for non-detection) and no longer contains the old unsatisfiable back-view sentence. The **Start over** control is visible during capture, its dialog opens, states what will happen, contains no em dash, has both buttons fully on screen (measured at y 455 to 497 in an 844px viewport), sits as a direct child of `<body>` with no transformed or filtered ancestor above it, and Cancel closes it and leaves the capture flow running. No JavaScript error anywhere.

One check failed on the first run and was wrong rather than the code: it scanned the bundle for "Step back until your entire body is visible" and found it. That string does still ship, but only as the one-time spoken setup hint played before validation starts, where it is accurate and competes with nothing. It is gone as a failure message, which is what mattered, but the two were the same string so a bundle scan cannot separate them. The check was replaced with an accurate one and the source-level fact is pinned in the unit tests instead.

## Fix: voice guidance could never be turned back on once blocked (2026-08-15)

**The report.** "The voice prompt is still not working."

**What was actually wrong.** Mobile browsers silently drop `speechSynthesis.speak()` calls that do not come from a user gesture, and a dropped call fires no events at all, so the only way to detect one is a watchdog: ask to speak, and if no "playing" event arrives within 1.5 seconds, conclude the call was refused. `hooks/useGuidedVoice.ts` does exactly that, and once it concluded "blocked" it stopped making further automatic attempts and the screen showed a "Tap once to enable voice guidance" button instead. All of that was correct.

**The defect was that the skip applied to every call, including the one made from inside that button's own tap handler.** So the recovery path was inert. The button appeared, the member tapped it, `speak()` returned before reaching the speech engine, no audio played, no "playing" event could arrive, and the blocked flag could never clear. Tapping again did the same thing. **Once blocked, voice guidance could never be turned back on for the rest of the assessment.**

Worse, the tap handler resumes the stalled intro script through a completion callback, and each skipped call still invoked that callback, so a single tap silently walked the entire remaining script in a few milliseconds without speaking a word of it, advancing the on-screen line to the last instruction as it went.

The same fault hit **all three** places a tap is supposed to make sound happen: the camera screen's recovery prompt, the prep screen's "Enable voice guidance" button, and the unmute control. That is why the member's experience was that voice simply never worked and no amount of pressing the button changed anything.

**The fix.** A user gesture is precisely the condition under which a blocked engine WILL accept a call, so it is the one case that must never be skipped for being blocked. New `lib/speech/speakGate.ts` holds that rule as a pure decision (`decideSpeak`, `shouldRetryBlocked`), separate from the hook so it is testable without a browser, a speech engine, or a React renderer. `speak()` gained a third argument, `{ fromUserGesture: true }`, passed at exactly the three tap sites and deliberately nowhere else: marking ordinary per-frame guidance as a gesture would defeat the blocked detection and put the member back to silence with no prompt to fix it.

A gesture call now also **clears** the blocked flag before speaking, so the watchdog re-arms and the outcome is learned honestly rather than assumed. If the engine refuses again, the flag comes straight back and the button reappears. Muting still wins over a gesture, since the unmute control clears `muted` first rather than speaking through it.

**Tests**: new `tests/voice-unblock.test.ts` (12). Six cover the decision itself, including that an automatic call is still skipped when blocked (that part was right and is worth keeping, since an automatic retry cannot succeed) while a gesture never is. The rest pin the wiring: that the hook routes through the gate rather than its own if-chain, that the flag is dropped BEFORE the decision is taken (dropping it after would leave the decision looking at a blocked state and skipping anyway), that all three tap sites are marked as gestures, and that the ready and capturing prompts are not.

**The deliberate break.** The gate was reverted to skipping every blocked call regardless of origin, which is the original bug exactly. The test named "NEVER skips a gesture call for being blocked, which is the whole fix" failed with `expected 'skip_blocked' to be 'speak'`. Reverted, and all pass.

**Observed but deliberately not changed.** A validation correction spoken while the fixed intro script is still playing cancels it, and the intro chain then stalls rather than resuming, because the generation guard correctly suppresses the cancelled utterance's completion callback. The member hears the first line or two of the script and then live corrections take over. That is a real rough edge, but it is arguably the right priority order (a live correction matters more than "Stand inside the outline"), it is a separate defect from the one reported, and fixing it would mean giving the intro script and the guidance machine a shared notion of who is speaking. Recorded here rather than folded in silently.

Full suite **5240 passing across 383 files**, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, production build compiled successfully. **No migration**: nothing here touches the database.

**Live verification against production** (commit `81e219f`, deployment `mef-platform-2jsqn1wxz`, target production, aliased to app.mefwellness.com; `scripts/screenshots/verify-capture-gate-live.mjs` extended, 390x844 iPhone viewport): **38/38 checks passed**.

A headless browser has a speech engine but no audio device, so **whether sound is audible cannot be checked here**. What can be checked is exactly the thing that was broken: whether a tap reaches the speech engine at all. `speechSynthesis.speak` is instrumented on a fresh page so every real call is counted, then the prep screen's voice control is driven for real. Tapping it took the counter from 1 to 2. Then, after waiting past the 1.5 second blocked-detection watchdog, **tapping it again took the counter from 3 to 4**, which is the behaviour that was impossible before: a second tap after the blocked flag had been raised used to be a guaranteed no-op.

Stated honestly, that live check is strong evidence rather than proof, because it cannot force the headless engine into the blocked state the way a real iPhone does. The logic itself is pinned conclusively by `tests/voice-unblock.test.ts`, which was shown to fail under the original behaviour. Also confirmed in the shipped bundle: the speak gate is present, and the "Tap once to enable voice guidance" prompt is still there for when it is needed. No JavaScript errors anywhere, and production was left as found.

## The Exercise Library and Movement Profile are internal tools now, and the protein ledger reads every lane (2026-08-16)

Two changes to what a member sees, and neither one needed a migration.

### The two movement tools left the member app

The Movement dashboard opened with three nav cards: Root Movement, Exercise Library, Movement Profile. Two of those three were coaching instruments wearing member clothes. The Exercise Library is a browsable catalog of every exercise in the system, and the Movement Profile is the permanent record a prescription is derived from. Both are gone from the member app, not locked and not teased: a member has no reason to know they exist.

**The gate is a mirror of the August 14 role routing, pointed the other way.** `lib/auth/staffRouting.ts` gained `STAFF_ONLY_PREFIXES` (`/exercises`, `/movement/profile`) alongside the `MEMBER_ONLY_PREFIXES` it already had, and one shared `matchesPrefix` boundary check now serves both. `isMemberOnlyPath` **subtracts** the staff-only list rather than the member list being hand pruned, which is what lets `/movement` keep owning its whole subtree in a single entry while `/movement/profile` is staff only. A path is one kind or the other and never both, so the two middleware gates cannot fight over the same request. Before that subtraction existed, a coach opening `/movement/profile` would have been bounced to `/coach` by the rule meant for member screens, because that path sits under the `/movement` member prefix. That case is a test.

**The failure posture is deliberately the opposite of the member-only rule's.** `hasActiveRole()` fails closed to false. For the member-only rule, false means "treat as a member", so a broken lookup leaves a member their whole app. For this rule, false means "redirect", so a broken lookup costs a coach one bounce to the Movement screen rather than opening an internal tool to a member. The consequence of being wrong is not symmetric, so the direction is not either.

**Gated twice, not once.** middleware.ts redirects, and each page independently calls `requireStaffForInternalTool()` (`lib/auth/staffOnlyPage.ts`) before it renders. These three pages sit outside the `/coach` and `/admin` route groups, at the URLs they held as member screens, so no layout carries the decision for them.

**Chrome followed the gate.** All three pages rendered `<BottomNav isCoach={...} />`, which is exactly the shape of the August 14 defect: an administrator who is not also a coach gets `false` and `false` draws the full member bar. They render `<StaffNav>` now, and `tests/staff-chrome-and-sign-out.test.ts`'s importer list was widened deliberately, with the reason recorded inline.

**Nothing was lost from the platform.** The coach dashboard reaches both tools, and so does the admin dashboard, so an administrator without the coach grant still has a way in. The real per-client tool was never on the member side and is untouched: a coach edits a client's Movement Profile from that client's own page (`app/coach/clients/[id]`, `MovementProfilePanel`).

**What a member keeps.** Everything her coach actually prescribed. `MovementExerciseCard` and `MovementSessionPlayer` render each exercise's media and cues in place and neither one routes through `/exercises`, which is a test rather than an assertion. The only other member-side references to either tool were the two cards themselves: a tree walk over `app/` and `components/` now fails the build if a link to either is ever added back to a member screen.

### The protein ledger already read most lanes. Now it reads all of them.

**First, what was already true, because it materially changes what this task was.** The ledger has never been a separate store. It is a protein-focused read over `member_food_log` (migration 59), the same table every logging path in this app writes to, and that was a deliberate decision recorded when it shipped on 2026-07-31. So a meal logged through the Food Lens barcode, label, search or manual lane, through a saved-meal repeat, or through "duplicate a previous meal" has always counted toward Today's Protein without being logged twice. Ten writers, one table, one read. The audit is written into `app/actions/protein-ledger.ts`'s header as a numbered list so it can be checked rather than trusted, and a test asserts each of those four action files still funnels through `insertFoodLogEntry`.

**The one lane that did not count, and why it looked broken.** The read carried `.not('product_id', 'is', null)`. Meal-photo entries are the only rows with a null product, so a member could photograph a meal, confirm every food in it, add it to her log, and find her protein ledger showing nothing at all. Not a zero against a logged meal: no trace that she had logged anything. The filter is gone. Those rows are read now, they appear in the day and in the 7-day history, and the entry says plainly that it is estimated from the photo and is not counted in grams.

**They contribute zero grams, and that is not a limitation to be fixed later, it is the rule.** Nothing in this application produces a gram figure from a photo. The vision provider returns a relative Low/Moderate/High read per meal (`food_lens_macro_estimates`), and `lib/food-lens/providers/types.ts` states the product rule directly: never a bare precise gram figure from a photo alone. So the ledger shows Root's relative read ("High protein") where a product-linked row shows a number, and the total does not move. Inventing grams to make a tally look complete would be the worst available outcome. If confirmed photo meals should ever carry grams, that needs a real source for them (per-item AI gram estimation, or a number the member enters herself), and it is a separate build with its own decisions.

**The mapping is pure now.** `buildLedgerEntries()` in `lib/protein/ledger.ts` takes rows plus three lookup maps and decides source, grams, name and relative level. The server action fetches; this decides. That is what let the integration tests run the shipped rule against real rows read through real RLS instead of testing a re-implementation of it, which is the failure mode a "does the ledger count this" test is most prone to.

**Dedup needed no dedup pass.** One `member_food_log` row is one ledger contribution, by construction. Two rows for the same product (a real duplicate-a-meal) are two contributions, which is correct, and is also a test.

### Proof

`tests/internal-movement-tools-staff-only.test.ts` (26) and `tests/protein-ledger-all-lanes.test.ts` (15). The sharp ones: a member, a coach and an administrator routed through the real seeded role grants rather than booleans typed into a test; staff-only and member-only proven mutually exclusive across the whole prefix list; the tree walk that finds any member-side link to either tool; a non-ledger-lane meal appearing exactly once in the total at its real grams; and a high-protein photo meal logged next to a 25g entry leaving the total at 25. Full suite: **5,325 passing** (two new files, one pre-existing typecheck error in `tests/hydration-focus.test.ts` fixed on the way through). Typecheck clean, lint clean (0 errors), production build clean. No migration.

**Live verification, run against app.mefwellness.com after the deploy went Ready and the domain was confirmed aliased to it.** Three Playwright scripts, kept in `apps/consumer-web-app/scripts/`:

- `verify-internal-tools-member-live.mjs` (6/6). Signed in as the production test member. The Movement screen renders Root Movement and nothing else: no Exercise Library, no Movement Profile. `/exercises`, `/movement/profile` and `/exercises/some-id` all land on `/movement`.
- `verify-protein-ledger-all-lanes-live.mjs` (6/6). Today's Protein started at 0g of 110g with "Nothing logged yet today." Logged a 31g food through Food Lens manual entry and its result screen's own Add to food log, which is not a ledger lane and never touches the ledger screen. Today's Protein read 31g, one entry, immediately. Then a 12g quick add through a ledger lane: 43g, two entries, and the 7-day history's Monday bar moved to 43g with it. Nothing counted twice.
- `verify-internal-tools-staff-live.mjs` (7/7). A real staff session, minted via generateLink/verifyOtp rather than a password and retired locally afterwards. Both tools open for a coach/administrator, both render the staff rail (Coach, Admin, Sign Out) rather than the member bottom bar, and both are linked from the coach dashboard and the admin dashboard.

**Left on the production test member deliberately**: the two entries that run created, "Live check food 04:05:02" (31g) and "Live check shake" (12g), so the result is visible on the real screen. Both are ordinary food log entries and can be removed with the trash icon on the ledger.

**Cosmetic, not fixed here**: a food typed through Food Lens manual entry is labeled "Scanned" in the ledger's entry list, because manual entry creates a `food_lens_scans` row (`scan_type: 'manual_entry'`) and `resolveEntrySource` reads only the presence of a scan id, not its type. Pre-existing, wrong in wording only, and telling it apart needs a scan-type join the ledger does not otherwise make.

## Trust cleanup: five things the app was telling members that were not true (2026-08-17)

The audit in `AUDIT-ADAPTIVE-REVEAL.md` found a lot. This pass fixed only the small, visible, provably-wrong ones. Nothing about scoring, interpretation or visibility was rebuilt; those are the next prompts, and everything the audit marked already compliant (the Priority Card decision engine, Case View, the safety tiering, the per-screen disclaimers) was left exactly as it was.

### A food a member logs is data, and it is no longer a finding about her

The Root Map was showing, under both Nutrition & Metabolic Health and Digestion & Gut Health, a bullet reading "Live check food 04:05:02: This product offers 31g of protein per serving..." That string is the name a verification script typed into Food Lens two weeks ago. It was on her wellness map with the same weight as an assessment finding because `lib/registry/adapters/foodProducts.ts` interpolated the product name straight into a registry finding narrative.

Deleting the row would have left the pipeline that produced it. Both food registry adapters are gone instead: `foodProducts.ts` (barcode and manual product analysis) and `foodLens.ts` (the meal-vs-pattern comparison, whose LLM narrative names the meal just as plainly, "That pistachio-vanilla matcha looks like a treat..."). Neither pipeline writes to `registry_entries` any more.

The scans themselves are untouched. `food_analysis_results`, `food_lens_pattern_comparisons` and `member_food_log` all still get written, the Food Lens result screen still shows the full analysis, and the protein ledger still reads every lane. What changed is that a single meal no longer becomes a standing, domain-attributed, permanent statement about the member's health. The one real cost is that Root's Conversation Coach and the Intelligence Engine no longer see food scans through the registry; the Coaching Intelligence Engine's nutrition source never did (it reads the comparison rows directly, which was always the better read) and is unaffected.

`RegistrySourceFeature` keeps both values, because 20 historical rows reference them, with a comment saying they are retired and must not come back. A test fails the build if either pipeline imports a registry adapter again, and a second test scans every surviving adapter for a `productName` argument.

### Every food-derived finding in production, retired

Twenty rows across three members, all set to `status: 'dismissed'`. **Zero deleted.** Four were live and member-facing; sixteen were already superseded and retired alongside them so none can resurface.

The four that were live on a member's screen:

| Recorded | Member | Row | What it said |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-17 | ab25b880 | `2d55f597-737e-400d-9f65-c1e33ef9ceb6` | "Live check food 04:05:02: This product offers 31g of protein per serving..." |
| 2026-08-16 | 3e7af809 | `adc7dbc3-5e16-49bc-bef1-5e8d5c9fae1f` | "Omelette: This omelette starts with a recognizable whole-food ingredient..." |
| 2026-08-16 | 3e7af809 | `6fa5c3ec-4765-4f47-bb42-0850f334922f` | "You haven't set up the real details of your eating pattern yet..." |
| 2026-07-31 | f37aa4a6 | `7bcd39ff-94fe-4422-825e-d31c2968ced4` | "That pistachio-vanilla matcha looks like a treat, but it's landing high on carbs..." |

The sixteen already-superseded rows retired with them: `c6fdf9c8`, `2013725e`, `3b3b59f8`, `144a9c50`, `9259a37f`, `892dc006` ("Western omelette with potatoes"), `13743d6a` ("Pasta bolognese"), `0177e0fc` ("Overnight oats with crushed chia, flax and hemp"), `37ab93b2` ("Chicken cutlets with marinara sauce"), `4dbe8e9b` ("Overnight oats, matcha granola"), `f91127ad` ("3 eggs, spinach, on sourdough bread"), `3d2b1344` ("Home made Italian Wedding Soup"), `7a32bd09` ("Egg, turkey, potato, wrap"), `ec08d050` ("Chicken cutlet Parmesan"), `c4dc4f46` ("Western omlet"), `0800ea7a` ("That iced matcha...").

### Only one thing can call itself today's coaching focus

Recommendations showed two cards, "Today's coaching focus: Stress" and "Today's coaching focus: Hydration", both saying "today". The dedup key for a focus row is built from its own title (`buildRecommendationKey`), the title contains the focus label, so Stress and Hydration were never the same key, the partial unique index on `(member, key) where status = 'shown'` never collided, and every focus the Brain had ever picked was still live.

Migration 164 adds a fifth lifecycle state, `superseded`. Deliberately not `expired` (that means "untouched for 30 days") and deliberately not `ignored` (that means the member said it wasn't helpful, which `outcomeHistory` reads as real negative feedback and which this system must never write on her behalf).

Two mechanisms, on purpose:

- **Write:** `retireSupersededCoachingFocus` runs at the end of every recompute and retires every focus row except the one that run just wrote.
- **Read:** `onlyCurrentCoachingFocus` keeps only the newest focus row at render time and passes everything else through untouched.

The second exists because the first can legitimately not happen. A coach viewing a client triggers the same recompute, and migration 91 gives a coach no UPDATE policy on a member's recommendations; every recompute is also best-effort and swallows its own errors. A display rule that depends on a write having succeeded is not a guarantee.

**Backfilled in production:** 13 stale rows across 6 members retired to `superseded`, 0 deleted. Twelve members had a live focus; the worst had six. Every member now has exactly one. The coach's Recommendations panel labels the retired ones "Replaced by a newer one" and still shows them, because that panel is the history view.

### A single mention is not a pattern

Coaching Insights headed a list "Patterns We're Beginning to Notice" and put "Discomfort: hips: We noticed this once." under it. The three-tier language module was right at the sentence level; the grouping above it overrode it.

`one_time_observation` now has its own group under "What We're Noticing So Far". Only `repeated_signal` and `emerging_pattern` sit under the pattern heading. The split is a pure function, `splitObservationsAndPatterns`, so it is tested rather than inspected.

### Nothing on a member screen states a confidence level

Home said "27 /100 · Steady · HIGH CONFIDENCE" while every one of the five domains underneath read "Building", because the roll-up's history term is `min(1, priorSnapshotCount / 5)` and snapshots accrue from a daily cron whether or not the member logs anything. After five days every member is maxed.

Every confidence label and percentage is off the member's screens: Home's hero, the Root Score line, the per-domain rows, and the four Food Lens surfaces (detected items, portion, macro meter, pattern comparison, label confirmation). `computeRootConfidence` and the per-domain coverage confidence are untouched and still running, so Prompt 2 has something to rebuild against.

Where a label was doing a real job it was replaced with the job rather than deleted. "Building your baseline" survives as a data statement, not a certainty claim.
